Each question is tagged to the curriculum topic it tests (content-folder/jamb-syllabus -> lib/notes/content/english-curriculum.ts). Seeding: scripts/seed-english-jamb-bank.mjs.

questions.question: Choose the option that is most nearly similar in meaning to the word: TENACIOUS
questions.explanation: Tenacious means holding firmly and not giving up — persistent. The other three share only a sound or a letter with the word.

questions.question: The minister's remarks were so CIRCUMSPECT that no one could tell which side he was on. The word CIRCUMSPECT means

options.text: Clearly stated and easy to follow

questions.explanation: The clue is the second half: no one could tell which side he was on. Circumspect means careful, wary, not committing oneself.

questions.question: Choose the option that is most nearly similar in meaning to the underlined word: 'The factory was IDLE for most of the quarter.'
questions.explanation: An idle factory is not operating. Unemployed describes people, untiring describes hard work, and unproductive would fit a factory that was working but yielding nothing.

questions.question: Choose the option that is most nearly similar in meaning to the word: 'The evidence against him was CIRCUMSTANTIAL.'

options.text: Based on inference rather than direct proof

questions.explanation: Circumstantial evidence points to a conclusion indirectly, by inference, rather than by direct testimony. It is not 'unimportant' — that is the trap.

questions.question: Choose the option that is most nearly similar in meaning to the word: 'The proposal was ABORTIVE.'
questions.explanation: Abortive means brought to nothing — it failed. Violent and delayed are not near-synonyms; expensive is not what the word means at all.

questions.question: Choose the option that is most nearly opposite in meaning to the word: GENEROUS
questions.explanation: The opposite of generous is miserly — stingy with money.

questions.question: Choose the option that is most nearly opposite in meaning to the word: 'The talks were FRUITLESS.'
questions.explanation: Fruitless means yielding nothing. The opposite is fruitful, yielding plenty.

questions.question: Choose the option that is most nearly opposite in meaning to the word: LUCID
questions.explanation: Lucid means clear in expression. Its opposite is obscure. Luminous and languid are near-lookalikes, not opposites.

questions.question: Choose the option that is most nearly opposite in meaning to the word: 'Despite the EXPEDIENT arrangement, the dispute dragged on for two years.'
questions.explanation: Expedient means suitable, convenient and speedy — the opposite here is something slow and awkward to arrange, that is cumbersome. Swift and temporary are near-synonyms of parts of the word, not its opposite.

questions.question: Choose the option that is most nearly opposite in meaning to the word: TENUOUS
questions.explanation: Tenuous means weak, slight and unconvincing. The opposite is strong. Slight and thin are near-synonyms; tense is unrelated.

questions.question: Choose the option that best explains the meaning of the expression: 'He was told to keep his nose to the grindstone.'

options.text: To finish a piece of work quickly

questions.explanation: The expression means to work with steady, undivided attention. It says nothing about speed, about avoiding mistakes, or about other people.

questions.question: Choose the option that best explains the meaning of the expression: 'The project died a natural death.'

options.text: It was abandoned without anyone deciding to abandon it
It ended because the sponsor withdrew
It was completed ahead of schedule

questions.explanation: To die a natural death means to stop gradually and without an explicit decision. The other options all describe a deliberate act, which is the opposite of the expression.

questions.question: Choose the option that best explains the meaning of the expression: 'He is a man of the moment.'

options.text: Someone currently influential or well suited to the present

questions.explanation: 'Of the moment' means current, belonging to the present time. In the image, the referee, the man of the moment, was the man whom the crowd was watching. The other options are literal readings that the idiom does not carry.

questions.question: Choose the option that best explains the meaning of the expression: 'After the audit, the department was made to toe the line.'

options.text: It was made to conform to the rules
It was made to draw a line under its accounts
It was made to line up its staff
It was made to pay the money it owed

questions.explanation: To toe the line means to behave as required, to conform. The other options take the words in their ordinary sense, which is exactly what a figurative expression does not mean.

questions.question: Choose the option that names the word class of the underlined word: 'The committee reached a decision after hours of DELIBERATION.'
questions.explanation: Deliberation is a noun — it names the act of thinking carefully. The preposition 'of' and the verb 'reached' show it is being used as the object of a preposition, which is a noun's job.

questions.question: Choose the option that names the word class of the underlined word: 'She sang BEAUTIFULLY.'
questions.explanation: Beautifully modifies the verb 'sang' and tells how she sang, so it is an adverb. An adjective would modify a noun — 'a beautiful song'.

questions.question: Choose the option that names the word class of the underlined word: 'The result was SURPRISING.'
questions.explanation: 'The result' is the subject and 'was' the verb, so the word between them describes the subject. A word describing a noun is an adjective, whatever its ending — 'an astonishing result' is an adjective too.

questions.question: Choose the option that names the word class of the underlined word: 'They were given a REWARD for their efforts.'
questions.explanation: 'A' before the word and 'for their efforts' after it make it the object of 'were given' — that is a noun's function.

questions.question: Choose the option that names the word class of the underlined word: 'He runs QUICKLY.'
questions.explanation: Quickly tells how he runs, so it modifies the verb and is an adverb. Note the trap: 'quick' as an adjective would need a noun — 'a quick run' — but here it stands alone after the verb.

questions.question: Choose the option that completes the sentence correctly: 'The list of approved suppliers (a) have (b) has (c) were (d) are submitted every quarter.'
questions.explanation: The subject is 'list', which is singular. The prepositional phrase 'of approved suppliers' sits between subject and verb and does not change the agreement.

questions.question: Choose the option that completes the sentence correctly: 'Neither the principal nor the two form teachers (a) was (b) were (c) is (d) are available for the meeting.'
questions.explanation: With 'neither ... nor', the verb agrees with the subject nearest to it. Here that is 'the two form teachers', so the verb is plural: were.

questions.question: Choose the option that completes the sentence correctly: 'The quality of the tomatoes (a) are (b) is (c) were (d) be poor this season.'
questions.explanation: The head of the subject is 'quality', singular. 'The tomatoes' is inside the prepositional phrase and does not control the verb.

questions.question: Choose the option that completes the sentence correctly: 'Each of the students (a) have (b) has (c) are (d) were given a certificate.'
questions.explanation: 'Each' is singular whatever follows it, so the verb is 'has'. The trap is that 'students' is plural and sits close to the verb — but the subject is 'each'.

questions.question: Choose the option that completes the sentence correctly: 'Mathematics (a) are (b) is (c) were (d) have always been his favourite subject.'
questions.explanation: Mathematics ends in -s but takes a singular verb, like 'physics' and 'news'. The ending of the word does not decide agreement; the word does.

questions.question: Choose the option that completes the sentence correctly: 'The report, together with the supporting documents, (a) are (b) is (c) were (d) have been submitted.'
questions.explanation: The head of the subject is 'report', singular. When a phrase beginning with 'together with' is added, it does not change the number of the subject.

questions.question: Choose the option that completes the sentence correctly: 'Hardly (a) the team had (b) had the team (c) had the team arrived (d) arrived when the news reached us.'
questions.explanation: With 'hardly' at the front of the clause, the auxiliary comes before the subject: 'Hardly had the team arrived'. Without the inversion, no mark.

questions.question: Choose the option that identifies the underlined part: 'When the bell rang, the pupils (a) filed out (b) of the classroom (c) quietly (d).'

options.text: The subject of the main clause

questions.explanation: 'The pupils' is who filed out, so it is the subject of the main clause. 'When the bell rang' is the subordinate clause.

questions.question: Choose the option that best completes the sentence: 'The book (a) which (b) that (c) who (d) I bought yesterday is out of print.'
questions.explanation: 'That' can refer to a thing as well as a person, and it is the safest choice. 'Who' and 'whom' are for people; 'which' is possible but 'that' is preferred here because the clause also takes an object ('I bought' takes 'it').

questions.question: Choose the option that completes the sentence correctly: 'Had I known the road was flooded, I (a) would have taken (b) would take (c) will take (d) had taken the other route.'
questions.explanation: 'Had I known' is the inverted past perfect for 'If I had known'. A third conditional past is completed by 'would have' plus a past participle.

questions.question: Choose the option that completes the sentence correctly: 'By the time the ambulance arrived, the driver (a) already recovered (b) has already recovered (c) had already recovered (d) was already recovering.'
questions.explanation: The recovery happened before the ambulance arrived, so the earlier of two past actions takes the past perfect.

questions.question: Choose the option that completes the sentence correctly: 'She (a) has been (b) had been (c) was (d) will be working on the report since Monday.'
questions.explanation: 'Since Monday' with a continuing action calls for the present perfect continuous: has been working.

questions.question: Choose the option that completes the sentence correctly: 'If I (a) were (b) am (c) have (d) had more time, I would join the expedition.'
questions.explanation: An unreal condition in the present uses the subjunctive 'were' for every person — 'if I were', 'if he were'. 'Am' is the indicative, which would state a real condition.

questions.question: Choose the option that completes the sentence correctly: 'The clerk informed us that the forms (a) will be (b) were (c) had been (d) are available from Monday.'
questions.explanation: A past reporting verb takes a past tense in the that-clause. The forms were available at the time of the telling.

questions.question: Choose the option that completes the sentence correctly: 'The road (a) has been (b) was (c) had been (d) will be resurfaced several times since it was built.'
questions.explanation: 'Since' with a repeated action up to now takes the present perfect: has been resurfaced several times.

questions.question: Choose the option that completes the sentence correctly: 'This is (a) the most quieter (b) the quieter (c) the quietest (d) quieter of the two pumps in the room.'
questions.explanation: Two things are being compared, so the comparative 'the quieter' is correct. Superlative would need three or more, and 'most' cannot be used with a word already ending in -er.

questions.question: Choose the option that completes the sentence correctly: 'The new road is (a) more wider (b) wider (c) much wider than (d) the old one.'
questions.explanation: Never double a comparative: not 'more wider'. 'Much' intensifies the comparative, and 'than' is required. The correct form is 'much wider than the old one'.

questions.question: Choose the option that completes the sentence correctly: 'Of the two, Adi's mark is (a) higher than (b) the highest than (c) more higher than (d) highest.'
questions.explanation: Two marks are being compared, so the comparative 'higher than'. 'Highest' is the superlative and does not take 'than'.

questions.question: Choose the option that completes the sentence correctly: 'Nothing in the store is (a) cheaper (b) more cheap (c) cheaper than (d) the one in the market.'
questions.explanation: Nothing in the store is cheaper than the one in the market. 'Cheaper' takes 'than' to complete the comparison, and 'more cheap' is a doubled comparative.

questions.question: Choose the option that best completes the sentence: 'It is the (a) most beautifully (b) beautifulest (c) most beautiful (d) beautiful of the paintings in the hall.'
questions.explanation: Three or more paintings, so the superlative: the most beautiful. 'Most' cannot stand with an adjective already ending in -ful, and 'beautifulest' is not a word.

questions.question: Choose the option that best completes the sentence: 'The contractors have finished the work, (a) have they? (b) haven't they? (c) have they not? (d) is it?'
questions.explanation: A positive statement takes a negative tag: 'have finished, have they?' A negative statement would take a positive tag, as in 'haven't finished, have they?'

questions.question: Choose the option that best completes the sentence: 'Nobody told them about the delay, (a) did they? (b) did nobody? (c) didn't they? (d) did no one?'
questions.explanation: Nobody is negative, so the tag is positive. The tag uses the ordinary pronoun 'they' for the subject 'nobody' — 'did they?'

questions.question: Choose the option that best completes the sentence: 'There isn't much food in the cupboard, (a) is there? (b) isn't there? (c) are there? (d) aren't there?'
questions.explanation: 'There' takes 'is' and the statement is negative, so the tag is positive: 'is there?'

questions.question: Choose the option that best completes the sentence: 'Let's begin the test, (a) shall we? (b) won't we? (c) will we? (d) don't we?'
questions.explanation: A suggestion with 'let's' takes the tag 'shall we?'

questions.question: Choose the option that best completes the sentence: 'You have been warned already, (a) have you? (b) haven't you? (c) had you? (d) do you?'
questions.explanation: The statement is positive and the auxiliary is 'have', so the tag repeats the auxiliary and flips the polarity: 'have you?'

questions.question: Choose the option that best completes the sentence: 'The committee have not reached a (a) decission (b) decision (c) desicion (d) dicision.'
questions.explanation: Decision — one 's', one 'c', and the '-tion' ending.

questions.question: Choose the option that correctly punctuates the sentence: 'The three candidates (a) Chidi, Tunde and Bisi (b) Chidi, Tunde, and Bisi (c) Chidi, Tunde and Bisi, (d) Chidi Tunde and Bisi arrived together.'
questions.explanation: A list of three takes a comma before the last 'and' only when the list is part of a larger sentence with more elements; in a simple list of three, the comma before 'and' is optional and normally left out. The comma after 'candidates' is required.

questions.question: Choose the option that correctly completes the sentence: 'The teachers (a) meeting (b) meetings (c) meeting's (d) meeting was held in the staff room.'
questions.explanation: 'The teachers meeting' is a noun phrase — the teachers who are meeting — so no apostrophe is needed. The apostrophe would only appear in a contraction such as 'the teachers' meeting room'.

questions.question: Choose the option that correctly punctuates the sentence: 'The governor declared (a) that the new road would be completed before the rains (b) that: the new road would be completed before the rains. (c) that the new road would be completed before the rains; (d) that the new road would be completed before the rains?'

options.text: that the new road would be completed before the rains
that: the new road would be completed before the rains.
that the new road would be completed before the rains;
that the new road would be completed before the rains?

questions.explanation: That-clauses take no colon, semicolon or question mark of their own — the punctuation belongs to the main sentence, which ends with a full stop.

questions.question: Choose the option that best completes the sentence: 'The officer gave a (a) seperate (b) separate (c) seperete (d) seperat briefing to each delegate.'
questions.explanation: Separate — 'se' then 'par' then 'ate'. The common misspelling puts the 'e' in the wrong place.

questions.question: Read the passage and answer the question. 'The queue outside the library had thinned to four people by nine o'clock. Inside, the last of the evening students were packing their bags, and the attendant was already running his closing checklist. He did not look up when the door opened, and the lights went off two minutes later.' The writer's attitude to the attendant is best described as

options.text: Unhurried and absorbed in his duties
Anxious about the length of the queue

questions.explanation: He was already running his checklist, so he was absorbed in his work, and he did not look up, so he was not hostile. The passage gives no sign of impatience or anxiety.

questions.question: Read the passage and answer the question. 'A borehole is not simply a hole. It is a hole, a casing, a pump, a power source and a maintenance plan. The first four can be installed in a fortnight. The fifth is what decides whether the borehole is still running in ten years.' The main point of the passage is that

options.text: A borehole lasts only if someone keeps it working
Boreholes take longer to install than people expect
Boreholes are more expensive than wells
Power supply is the hardest part of a borehole

questions.explanation: The fifth element, the maintenance plan, is the one that decides the outcome. The passage is about what keeps a borehole alive, not about cost, power or installation time.

questions.question: Read the passage and answer the question. 'The proposal met with stiff opposition from the council, and after two postponements it was quietly dropped.' The word 'quietly' suggests that the proposal was
questions.explanation: Quietly marks the opposite of an announcement. Combined with 'was dropped', it points to the proposal disappearing without a formal decision being made public.

questions.question: Read the passage and answer the question. 'He was the kind of man who arrived early, helped without being asked, and left before anyone thought to thank him.' The writer suggests that the man

options.text: Expected to be thanked for his help
Was afraid of being seen by his colleagues
Had been trained to serve without speaking

questions.explanation: He left before anyone could thank him, so he was not seeking recognition. Nothing in the passage suggests fear or a rule requiring silence.

questions.question: Read the passage and answer the question. 'The hall has a ceiling of forty iron trusses, each painted a different shade of green, and a floor of worn brown tiles that click under every heel. Along the north wall, twelve tall windows have lost their paint, so the light that enters is already old.' According to the passage, the light entering the hall is described as

options.text: Faded and weakened by the windows' lost paint
Bright and reflected from the green ceiling
Warm because it is late in the afternoon
Dim because the floor is dark

questions.explanation: 'The light that enters is already old' — old meaning faded. The lost paint on the windows is the stated cause. Nothing in the passage mentions the time of day or the green ceiling causing the light.

questions.question: Read the passage and answer the question. 'Behind the workshop, past the stack of offcuts and the half-burnt brazier, the yard is a hundred square metres of packed red earth. It is where the goats are kept, where the tyres are burnt, and where, in the dry season, the dust reaches the verandah and settles on everything, including the television.' The passage mainly describes

options.text: A yard that is useful, neglected and dusty
A workshop where furniture is produced
A television that has been left outdoors
A village with no system of waste disposal

questions.explanation: The yard is used for several purposes, is not cared for, and fills with dust — a description of one place in all its aspects. The other options each pick a single element and generalise beyond the passage.

questions.question: Read the passage and answer the question. 'The old press squeals each time the handle comes down, then the flywheel takes over with a low hum that you feel more than hear. A smell of hot oil and old cotton hangs in the air.' The writer's use of 'you feel more than hear' is to convey

options.text: That the sound is low and the vibration is physical
That the machine is running too fast to be safe
That the workshop is unusually quiet
That the writer is imagining the sound

questions.explanation: The phrase contrasts hearing with feeling: the hum is so low and the vibration so strong that the body registers it. It is a precise sensory claim, not a statement about speed, quietness or imagination.

questions.question: Read the passage and answer the question. 'A single mango tree stands where the courtyard used to be. The new block is four floors of cream concrete with blue railings, and the balconies are stacked with laundry in every colour of a market. On the ground floor, a tailor works behind a sheet of polythene, and a woman sells cold pepper from a plastic bowl.' The description mainly serves to show

options.text: How the old courtyard has been replaced by a busy, lived-in block
That the neighbourhood has improved since the tree was felled
That the residents prefer the old courtyard
That the block was built without planning

questions.explanation: The details accumulate: the tree is gone, the block is new, and life has moved into it. The passage describes change, not improvement or preference — those would be judgements the text does not make.

questions.question: Read the passage and answer the question. 'The bell had not rung when Amaka reached the gate. She sat on the low wall, counting buses. At seven the buses began to come, but the road was already thick with cars. By the time the yard opened, the morning had turned grey and she had counted forty-one.' Which order does the passage give?

options.text: Amaka arrives, the buses start coming, the yard opens
The yard opens, Amaka arrives, the buses start coming
The buses start coming, Amaka arrives, the yard opens
Amaka arrives, the yard opens, the buses start coming

questions.explanation: 'The bell had not rung when Amaka reached the gate' comes first, then 'At seven the buses began to come', then 'By the time the yard opened'. A narration is read as a chain, and this one is strictly chronological.

questions.question: Read the passage and answer the question. 'The engine coughed twice and died. For a moment nothing happened, and then the man in the back seat began to laugh — a short, helpless laugh that turned into something else. The driver turned round to look at him.' The turning point of the narrative is the moment

options.text: The man in the back seat begins to laugh
The engine coughs for the second time
The driver turns round to look

questions.explanation: The engine failing is the set-up, not the turn — the situation is still as expected. The laugh is what changes the mood, and it is what makes the driver turn round.

questions.question: Read the passage and answer the question. 'My father did not look at me when he said it. He said it to the window, the way he said everything that mattered, and then he put the keys on the table and went out of the room.' The passage suggests that the father

options.text: Found the words difficult to say to his child directly
Was angry with the child and wanted to leave
Had forgotten what he wanted to say
Was in a hurry to go out

questions.explanation: The writer notes two habits — not looking, and speaking to the window for things that matter — and neither is explained. The inference is that the words were hard to deliver face to face. Nothing suggests anger, forgetfulness or haste.

questions.question: Read the passage and answer the question. 'The bell rang, the crowd stood, the doors opened, and the whole street emptied into the hall in the space of a minute. Afterwards there was no conversation for a long time.' The mood the final sentence creates is
questions.explanation: The sentence reports the absence of conversation, and the flatness of the reporting matches it. Nothing in the passage celebrates or alarms.

questions.question: Read the passage and answer the question. 'First, the seed coat must be broken by water. Once the water has reached the embryo, the cells begin to divide and the radicle pushes downwards. Only then does the shoot rise, seeking light. The order cannot be reversed: a shoot that rises before the root has formed will not survive.' The last sentence exists to

options.text: Show that the steps depend on each other and must happen in sequence
Give an example of what happens when a seed is sown too deeply
Explain why light matters to a growing shoot
Warn readers against growing plants indoors

questions.explanation: The sentence says the order cannot be reversed, and gives a consequence of reversing it. It is about the dependency between the steps, not about depth, light or indoor growing.

questions.question: Read the passage and answer the question. 'The most effective way to preserve a tomato is to keep it cold and keep it dry. Cold slows the enzyme reactions that turn starch into sugar, and dry keeps the mould from finding the water it needs. Above eight degrees the changes become visible within a day.' According to the passage, mould grows best when the tomato is
questions.explanation: Dry keeps mould from finding the water it needs, and temperatures above eight degrees speed the changes. So mould is worst off when the tomato is warm and wet.

questions.question: Read the passage and answer the question. 'A simple water filter can be built in an afternoon. The first stage removes the sediment: the water is poured through a cloth, catching the sand and grit. The second stage deals with what the cloth let through.' The phrase 'The second stage' tells the reader that

options.text: Another step in the same process is being described
The filter has exactly two parts
The writer disagrees with the first stage
The second stage is the more important one

questions.explanation: It is a signpost moving the explanation along to the next stage. It does not claim there are only two stages, and it says nothing about importance.

questions.question: Read the passage and answer the question. 'A generator that idles for hours wastes fuel and wears faster than one that runs at full load for the same number of hours. The calculation that surprises most people is that the fuel saved by switching off a diesel engine after five minutes of idling is small; the wear saved is not.' The passage implies that

options.text: The case for switching off an engine rests on wear rather than fuel
Generators should never be allowed to idle
Fuel is the main cost of running a generator
Idling engines last longer than fully loaded ones

questions.explanation: The passage says the fuel saving is small and the wear saving is not, so the real argument is about wear. It stops short of saying generators should never idle, and it says nothing about fuel being the main cost.

questions.question: Read the passage and answer the question. 'It is fashionable to blame the school bag for the traffic. The bag is heavier than it was; the bus is slower than it was; therefore the bag must go. But a bag that is lighter does not make a bus arrive sooner, and a bus that is earlier does not make a bag lighter. The two problems are real and they are not the same problem.' The writer's argument is that

options.text: Traffic and the weight of school bags are separate problems that need separate solutions
School bags should be made of lighter materials
Buses should be made faster in city centres
The fashion of blaming school bags should end

questions.explanation: The two sentences about the bag and the bus show that solving one does not solve the other, and the last sentence states they are not the same problem. Options B, C and D each take only a fragment.

questions.question: Read the passage and answer the question. 'Some people say the examination was too long. It was. But the complaint is not really about length; it is about the weight of the last two questions, which nobody can finish in the time given.' The writer concedes that

options.text: The last two questions were badly set
Candidates should be given more time

questions.explanation: 'It was' immediately after 'the examination was too long' is the concession — the writer agrees — and then immediately disputes the significance of that agreement.

questions.question: Read the passage and answer the question. 'We could close the market on Sundays. It would be tidier, and the traders would lose a morning of trade. Some of them would lose a morning of trade they cannot afford to lose. Tidier, then, is not the whole of it.' The writer's purpose in the last two sentences is to

options.text: Acknowledge a real benefit while refusing to treat it as decisive
End the argument by recommending that the market close
Show that closing the market would be impossible

questions.explanation: 'Tidier' is granted, and 'but' then introduces the cost, and the closing sentence concedes that tidiness does not settle the matter. That is a concession used to limit a conclusion, not a recommendation.

questions.skill: figures of speech in an argument
questions.question: Read the passage and answer the question. 'You cannot make the horse drink and then complain that it will not drink. The argument is the same: build the road first, then ban the lorry.' The image of the horse is used to

options.text: Present the objection as a familiar absurdity so that it can be dismissed
Describe how horses are trained to drink
Suggest that road building is as old as horse rearing
End the passage on a note of gentle humour

questions.explanation: The proverb is used to show that the objection is confused rather than serious. It is an argument, not a joke: the point is that you cannot demand a result before creating the condition for it.

questions.question: Read the passage and answer the question. 'Every Tuesday, twelve women meet in the back room of a barber's shop to learn how to read and write. The barber lends the room for an hour because his mother is among them. In three years, nine of the twelve have started small businesses of their own. The remaining three still attend every week.' Which summary best captures the passage?

options.text: A weekly literacy class that has led most of its members into small business
A barber who is frustrated by the use of his shop for a literacy class
Twelve women who failed to find work and started a school together
A literacy class that is about to close because of falling attendance

questions.explanation: A summary must carry the main point — the class, and what most of its members did next. The passage says nothing about frustration, about the members being unemployed, or about the class closing; option D also contradicts the fact that all twelve still attend.

questions.question: Read the passage and answer the question. 'The old bridge was closed in 2019 after a routine inspection found corrosion in two of the load-bearing joints. A new bridge was approved the same year, and work began in 2021. The new bridge opened to traffic in March of this year, and the old one is now scheduled for demolition.' Which summary best captures the passage?

options.text: A corroded bridge was closed and has been replaced by a new one now in use
The old bridge was demolished and traffic was redirected for two years
Corrosion was found in the new bridge shortly after it opened
The council rejected the proposal for a replacement bridge

questions.explanation: Each option has to be checked against the passage. B is wrong because the old bridge has not yet been demolished. C is wrong because the corrosion was in the old bridge. D is wrong because the new bridge was approved. Only A states what the passage actually says.

questions.skill: summary of a passage with detail
questions.question: Read the passage and answer the question. 'Reading the labels on food in a Nigerian shop, you will find that the commonest sweetener is a syrup made from maize starch, sold under names that sound foreign. Many buyers assume it is sugar. It is not: it is glucose, and the body treats it differently. A handful of the products do contain cane sugar, and they cost about a fifth more.' Which summary best captures the passage?

options.text: Many shoppers mistake cheaper maize-based glucose for sugar, while genuine cane sugar costs more
Glucose is healthier than sugar and should be bought instead
Most food labels in Nigeria are false and should be ignored
The government has banned the sale of maize syrup in shops

questions.explanation: A summary keeps what the passage establishes: the assumption, the correction, and the price difference. Options B, C and D each introduce a claim — a health recommendation, a general judgement about labelling, and a ban — that the passage never makes.

questions.question: Read the passage and answer the question. 'For three weeks the rain did not stop. On the fourth morning the river came over the road at the ford, and by noon it had reached the door of the school. The children walked four miles to a school under a tree, where the lessons continued until the water came for that too.' A summary in one sentence should NOT include

options.text: That the children continued to be taught somewhere else
That the flood eventually reached the school
The exact number of days it rained
That the river overflowed onto the road

questions.explanation: A summary in one sentence keeps the main points — the flood, the move, and the continuation of schooling — and drops detail. The precise number of days is exactly the kind of detail that has to go.

questions.question: Read the passage and answer the question. 'The samples were (1)____ for two hours before the test began, and the temperature was not allowed to (2)____ by more than two degrees.' Gap 1: A vary, B change, C exchange, D alternate. Gap 2: A move, B float, C rise, D fall.
questions.explanation: Gap 1 wants a word meaning to shift or fluctuate over time: 'changed for two hours'. Gap 2 wants a word for going up, and 'not allowed to rise' is the fixed collocation in a control of this kind. 'Fall' would need 'by more than' to mean a downward movement, but the passage's sense is of drift in either direction, and 'rise' is the standard term here.

questions.question: Read the passage and answer the question. 'Although the drug (1)____ the symptoms within a day, it does not (2)____ the cause of the illness.' Gap 1: A relieves, B releases, C relieves, D lends. Gap 2: A affect, B effect, C cure, D accept.
questions.explanation: 'Relieve the symptoms' is the fixed collocation, and 'affect the cause' — not 'effect', which is a noun — completes the contrast between symptom and cause. The passage is making a distinction, and the grammar has to match it.

questions.question: Read the passage and answer the question. 'The results of the trial were (1)____ with those of the earlier study, and the researchers (2)____ a larger sample before drawing any conclusion.' Gap 1: A consistent, B consisted, C consisted, D persistent. Gap 2: A urged, B called, C demanded, D suggested.
questions.explanation: 'Results' is plural, so gap 1 is the adjective 'consistent'. Gap 2 takes an object: 'called for a larger sample' is the fixed expression meaning demanded. 'Suggested' and 'urged' do not take 'for' in this sense.

questions.question: Read the passage and answer the question. 'The scheme was extended to two more states, but the funds (1)____ available were not enough to (2)____ the number of clinics promised.' Gap 1: A actually, B only, C merely, D solely. Gap 2: A support, B uphold, C sustain, D supply.
questions.explanation: Gap 1 needs a word that contrasts with the expectation of plenty: 'actually'. Gap 2 needs a verb meaning to keep going over time: 'sustain the number'. 'Supply' would need 'the clinics' rather than 'the number of clinics'.

questions.question: Choose the option that has the SAME vowel sound as the word: seat
questions.explanation: Seat and beat both carry the long /i/ sound. Bit has /i/, bet has /e/, and sat has /ae/.

questions.question: Choose the option that has the SAME vowel sound as the word: chair
questions.explanation: Chair and hair both begin with the /e/ diphthong as in 'air'. Ride and raid have /ai/, rid has /i/.

questions.question: Choose the option that has the SAME vowel sound as the word: light
questions.explanation: Light and pipe share the /ai/ sound. Lip and leap are closer spelled but carry /i/, and keep carries /i/ too.

questions.question: Choose the option that has the SAME vowel sound as the word: head
questions.explanation: Head and bread both contain the short /e/ sound. Bead has /i/, bid has /i/, and broad has a long /o/.

questions.question: Choose the option that has the SAME vowel sound as the word: song
questions.explanation: Song and long share the short /o/ sound before -ng. Sing has /i/, sang has /ae/, sung has the rough /ah/.

questions.question: Choose the option that has the SAME vowel sound as the word: blood
questions.explanation: Blood and flood both say /ah/ even though 'oo' is written. Good and hood say /oo/ as in foot, and food sounds like 'fo' with long u.

questions.question: Choose the option that begins with the SAME consonant sound as the word: chair
questions.explanation: Chair and child both begin with the /ch/ sound. Kite has /k/, sheet has /sh/, and skirt begins with /sk/.

questions.question: Choose the option that begins with the SAME consonant sound as the word: gate
questions.explanation: Gate and goat both begin with the hard /g/ sound. Plate begins with /pl/, cat with /k/, and dot with /d/.

questions.question: Choose the option that begins with the SAME consonant sound as the word: ship
questions.explanation: Ship and sheet both begin with /sh/. Sip and sick begin with /s/, and chip begins with /ch/.

questions.question: Choose the option that begins with the SAME consonant sound as the word: window
questions.explanation: Window and wings both begin with /w/. Vowel begins with /v/, night with /n/, and wrong with /r/.

questions.question: Choose the option that begins with the SAME consonant sound as the word: knight
questions.explanation: The k in knight is silent, so the word opens with /n/ like knee. Write opens with /r/, key with /k/, and lamb with /l/.

questions.question: Choose the option that begins with the SAME consonant sound as the word: physics
questions.explanation: Physics and phone both begin with /f/ even though physics is spelled with 'ph'. Laugh begins with /l/, screen with /sk/, and stone with /st/.

questions.question: Choose the option that RHYMES with the word: light
questions.explanation: Light and night rhyme because they share the vowel plus everything after it. Lamb, page, and lot all carry different endings.

questions.question: Choose the option that RHYMES with the word: cat
questions.explanation: Cat and bat rhyme exactly. Cut and cot carry different vowels, and can is short a followed by n.

questions.question: Choose the option that RHYMES with the word: far
questions.explanation: Far and star are perfect rhymes. Fat ends short, fear dips, and fur carries a crooked r-sound it does not share.

questions.question: Choose the option that RHYMES with the word: cold
questions.explanation: Cold and hold share the long o and the closing ld. 'Code' stops at d, could and world carry different sounds entirely.

questions.question: Choose the option that RHYMES with the word: stone
questions.explanation: Stone and phone both end in the long o plus n. Strong carries a short o, shout dips, and shut is short.

questions.question: Choose the option that RHYMES with the word: heat
questions.explanation: Heat and seat end with the same long e plus t. Hide, hate, and hat all lean on different sounds at the front.

questions.question: Which syllable carries the MAIN stress in the word: photography
questions.explanation: The main stress falls on the second syllable: pho-TO-graphy. The first and last syllables ring quieter by comparison.

questions.question: Which syllable carries the MAIN stress in the word: certificate
questions.explanation: The main stress falls on the final syllable: cer-tif-fi-CATE. The first syllable carries a softer, secondary stress.

questions.question: Which syllable carries the MAIN stress in the word: committee
questions.explanation: The main stress falls on the second syllable: com-MIT-tee. The first syllable is secondary, the last is weak.

questions.question: Which syllable carries the MAIN stress in the word: education
questions.explanation: The main stress falls on the third syllable: ed-u-CA-tion. The ending 'tion' is always weak.

questions.question: Which syllable carries the MAIN stress in the word: overlap
questions.explanation: The main stress falls on the first syllable: OV-er-lap. Over then carries a lighter stress at the end.

questions.question: Which syllable carries the MAIN stress in the word: physical
questions.explanation: The main stress falls on the second syllable: phy-SI-cal.

questions.question: Which word would you stress to show emphasis in: 'I DID tell you so.'
questions.explanation: Stressing 'did' answers a denial: it insists the telling really happened. The other words make no contrast.

questions.question: Which word would you stress to show emphasis in: 'THEY told you so.'
questions.explanation: Stressing 'they' points the blame away from the speaker: it was them, not me, who told you.

questions.question: Which word would you stress to show emphasis in: 'I saw it with my OWN eyes.'
questions.explanation: Stressing 'own' adds 'by myself personally'. It divides the seeing from listening or hearing about it.

questions.question: Which word would you stress to show emphasis in: 'The manager HIMSELF told me.'
questions.explanation: Stressing 'himself' adds that no middle man was in the chain. It proves the information came from the top.

questions.question: Which word would you stress to show emphasis in: 'I said TWO, not three.'
questions.explanation: Stressing 'two' contrasts it against the wrong figure, 'three'. It is the number itself that is being defended.

questions.question: Which word would you stress to show emphasis in: 'WE live in Lagos.'
questions.explanation: Stressing 'Lagos' divides it from other places: we live here, not anywhere else. The place is the point being defended.

questions.question: Read the passage and answer the question. 'When words are unclear, clear thought and communication require a method of fixing their meanings. One traditional method is to state the general class to which a term belongs and the particular attribute that separates it from every other member of that class. A whale, for instance, is a marine animal that spouts. Examples can also indicate what a term covers, but that device is of limited use: after the examples of animals, for instance, one may still not know whether a sea anemone or a slug counts.' What is the passage mainly about?

options.text: How words can be clearly defined
How mammals differ from sea creatures

questions.explanation: The passage is about how to give words a fixed meaning: class and distinguishing property first, examples as a supplement.

questions.question: Read the passage and answer the question. 'When words are unclear, clear thought and communication require a method of fixing their meanings. One traditional method is to state the general class to which a term belongs and the particular attribute that separates it from every other member of that class. A whale, for instance, is a marine animal that spouts.' In the definition of a whale, what does 'marine animal' indicate?

options.text: An example of a marine animal

questions.explanation: The writer says the class is like 'marine animal'; the distinguishing property is 'spouts'.

questions.question: Read the passage and answer the question. 'When a word is not certain, we may have to enumerate examples to indicate what it includes, but that device is of limited usefulness. If we illustrated the word 'animal' with rabbit, dog, fish or goat, our hearers might still doubt whether a sea anemone or a slug should be included.' Why is enumerating examples of limited usefulness?

options.text: It takes too long to prepare
It is useful only for mammals
It does not settle doubtful cases
It always includes every member of a class

questions.explanation: The examples leave borderline cases uncertain, so hearers may still be unsure where the class ends.

questions.question: Read the passage and answer the question. 'Examples can supplement a definition if the definition itself is definite without being easily understandable.' According to the passage, when are examples useful?

options.text: When the examples are hard to recognise
When a meaning is already clear
When a term has no class
When the definition is exact but hard to grasp

questions.explanation: The writer says examples are helpful when a definition is precise but difficult to understand.

questions.question: Read the passage and answer the question. 'One method of indicating the meaning of a term is enumerating examples of what it includes.' In the passage, 'enumerating' most nearly means:
questions.explanation: To enumerate examples is to list the items that a term includes.

questions.question: Read the passage and answer the question. 'Nigerian reading culture is said to be at a low ebb. Few readers prefer foreign books, and many Nigerian authors complain that bookshop owners and publishers treat them badly. One bookseller explains that foreign books are stocked because demand is higher. Yet Nigerian writers have won international honours: Chimamanda Ngozi Adichie, Chinua Achebe, Wole Soyinka and Ben Okri are named as examples. The writer asks why Nigerians do not give their own authors similar recognition at home.' What is the passage mainly about?

options.text: The reasons why publishers reject Nigerian books
Why foreign books are always better than local books
The weakness of reading culture in Nigeria and the neglect of Nigerian authors
How international awards are shared among writers

questions.explanation: The passage links a weak reading culture with the neglect of Nigerian authors despite their international honours.

questions.question: Read the passage and answer the question. 'One bookseller explains that foreign books are stocked because demand is higher. The writer nevertheless asks why Nigerians do not give their own authors similar recognition at home.' According to the passage, what reason do bookshops give for stocking many foreign books?

options.text: Their books are in greater demand

questions.explanation: The bookseller says foreign books are stocked because more customers demand them.

questions.question: Read the passage and answer the question. 'Chimamanda Ngozi Adichie won the Orange Prize, Chinua Achebe won the Man Booker International Prize, Wole Soyinka won the Nobel Prize for Literature, and Ben Okri won the Booker Prize.' What do these examples establish?

options.text: Nigerian writers have reached the highest levels of world literature
Foreign books are less popular in Nigeria

questions.explanation: The named prizes show that the writers have won the world's most honoured literary awards.

questions.question: Read the passage and answer the question. 'While Nigerian authors are rewarded with international honours, why are Nigerians not according them such recognition in their own country?' What question most fully represents the authors' complaint?

options.text: Why is the reading culture weak?
Why do bookshops prefer foreign books?
Why are they honoured abroad but not recognised by Nigerians?
Why are awards given to Nigerian writers?

questions.explanation: The central complaint is the contrast between foreign honour and missing recognition at home.

questions.question: Read the passage and answer the question. 'In essence, the reading culture in Nigeria is now at a low ebb.' In the passage, 'at a low ebb' most nearly means:
questions.explanation: A low ebb means falling or weakened; here the reading culture is reported to be declining.

questions.question: Read the passage and answer the question. 'People say experience is the best teacher, but learning through wisdom can be more convenient. Learning only from experience means learning from mistakes, and that route is difficult, costly and inconvenient. A person should decide to learn consciously, devoting himself to new knowledge each day, rather than wait for a mistake to force the lesson.' What is the writer's main argument?

options.text: Learning through wisdom is preferable to learning only through mistakes
Mistakes are necessary for every learner
Experience is more useful than wisdom

questions.explanation: The writer presents wisdom as a conscious, better alternative to costly learning by experience.

questions.question: Read the passage and answer the question. 'Learning by experience is to learn from mistakes. It means you have burnt your fingers and now your eyes are open. This is a tough, costly and inconvenient way to learn.' Why does the writer call this way of learning inconvenient?
questions.explanation: Learning by experience is presented as learning after the mistake has already been made.

questions.question: Read the passage and answer the question. 'If we decide to learn today, we must couple our decision with complete and wholehearted devotion. We must be resolved, resolute and resilient, and learn something new every day.' What does the writer say should follow the decision to learn?
questions.explanation: The decision must be backed by full commitment and carried out through new learning each day.

questions.question: Read the passage and answer the question. 'Life is the outcome and outplay of decisions. Our life now is the sum total of our decisions, and our future will be determined by the decisions we make today.' What can be inferred from the passage?

options.text: Decisions have no effect on later life

questions.explanation: Because life is said to be the sum total of decisions, today's choices shape tomorrow.

questions.question: Read the passage and answer the question. 'We must be resolved, resolute and resilient in our bid to learn by wisdom.' In this context, 'resolute' most nearly means:
questions.explanation: A resolute person is decided and firm, resolved to keep to the chosen course.

questions.question: Read the passage and answer the question. 'A university is restructuring its approach road to ease the flow of traffic, strengthen security and give the institution an appropriate introduction. The Works and Services Complex is also under construction. The projects are designed with aesthetics and a healthy environment in mind because beauty affects inhabitants psychologically and socially. The announcement asks people to bear temporary diversions and inconveniences while development proceeds. Finally, it assures the government that the university can manage and spend project funds quickly.' What is the main purpose of the passage?

options.text: To persuade the public to donate to the university
To describe the university's new roads and buildings
To explain the projects, temporary inconvenience and capacity to spend funds
To explain why the university needs more roads

questions.explanation: The passage itemises current development, warns of temporary inconvenience, and assures the government of execution capacity.

questions.question: Read the passage and answer the question. 'The projects are being executed with an eye to aesthetics for we recognize the important influence of a beautiful and healthy environment of its inhabitants.' Why are the projects designed with aesthetics?

options.text: A healthy environment benefits inhabitants psychologically and socially
Security is easier in an ugly environment
Traffic flows better when buildings are beautiful

questions.explanation: The writer says a beautiful, healthy environment has a beneficial psychological and sociological effect.

questions.question: Read the passage and answer the question. 'We appeal to you to bear with us in full knowledge that such inconveniences are temporary and will soon yield final tangible results.' How are readers to regard the inconvenience?

options.text: As temporary and followed by real results
As a reason to abandon the projects

questions.explanation: The writer says the inconveniences are temporary and will yield final tangible results.

questions.question: Read the passage and answer the question. 'I can assure Government that its ability to disburse funds to us will be more than matched by our capacity to collect and expend them on executing various worthy projects in record time.' What assurance is the writer giving the government?

options.text: The government should disburse all its funds
The university can collect and spend project funds quickly

questions.explanation: The assurance is that the university can receive funds and turn them into completed projects promptly.

questions.question: Read the passage and answer the question. 'The projects are being executed with an eye to aesthetics.' In the passage, 'aesthetics' most nearly means:
questions.explanation: Aesthetics concerns beauty; the projects are designed to look and feel suitable.

questions.question: Read the passage and answer the question. 'By age two, psychologists say a child is self-conscious. The psychologist means that the child is aware that he is a self and not an extension of his mother. This awareness is shown in such behavioural acts as disobedience and the use of the word No with emphasis.' According to the passage, what does 'self-conscious' mean in the psychologist's sense?

options.text: The child knows he is a separate self
The child is shy before strangers
The child thinks only of himself

questions.explanation: The psychological meaning is awareness of being a self separate from the mother.

questions.question: Read the passage and answer the question. 'This awareness is shown in such behavioural acts as disobedience and the use of the word No with emphasis, because the child is aware that he does not have to obey parental commands.' Which behaviour shows the child's self-awareness?
questions.explanation: The writer gives disobedience and emphatic use of 'No' as evidence of the new awareness.

questions.question: Read the passage and answer the question. 'Parental commands are first for the child's own safety and secondly so the child begins to develop a sense of right and wrong. The young child lacks a developed concept of time and is governed by immediate desires which must be fulfilled.' Why can a young child sometimes be excused for not behaving morally?

options.text: He is afraid of his parents
He already knows right from wrong
He has no developed concept of time

questions.explanation: Because the child cannot yet weigh future consequences, immediate desires may govern him.

questions.question: Read the passage and answer the question. 'In some situations, the young child can be excused for not behaving morally. In other situations, he knows what is right and chooses not to do it. Immature adults can also behave in this way.' What does the passage suggest about the immature adult?

options.text: He may act in his own interest like a child
He never understands right from wrong
He lacks a concept of time altogether

questions.explanation: The writer compares the immature adult with the child who knowingly chooses self-interest.

questions.question: Read the passage and answer the question. 'The young child is governed by immediate desires which must be fulfilled. Immature adults can also behave in this self-centred way.' As used in the passage, 'self-centred' most nearly means:

options.text: Preoccupied with oneself and one's immediate desires

questions.explanation: Self-centred here means acting from one's own immediate interest rather than a wider moral consideration.

questions.question: Read the passage and answer the question. 'The young are not listening to their elders for a medical reason: many cannot hear. Hearing specialists report that youngsters are going deaf as a result of electronically amplified music. Loud noise was once linked with deafness in industrial and military settings; continuous boiler-factory noise can cause permanent hearing loss, and jets exposed ground crews and aircraft carriers. In concerts, the problem is less the instruments or the close quarters than the electronic amplifiers.' What is the passage mainly arguing?

options.text: All young people have stopped listening
Musical instruments are dangerous by nature
Hearing loss is a new problem everywhere
Amplified music, more than instruments or closeness, endangers young hearing

questions.explanation: The writer traces the danger to electronic amplification, not to instruments or close quarters.

questions.question: Read the passage and answer the question. 'Hearing specialists used to worry about loud noise as a cause of deafness only in industrial and military situations. Continuous exposure to the din of a boiler factory would eventually cause permanent hearing loss.' Which setting is given as an example of a noise hazard?
questions.explanation: The boiler factory is named as a classic industrial deafness hazard, along with military settings.

questions.question: Read the passage and answer the question. 'An old-fashioned military band generated as much sound as an amplified one, but the sound was not amplified and was dissipated in the open air. A trombonist near a tuba player might be slightly deaf for an hour or so; then his hearing returned to normal.' Why was the older military band less dangerous?

options.text: The sound was unamplified and dispersed outdoors
The band played only with recorders

questions.explanation: Because the sound was not amplified and spread out in the open air, the effect was temporary.

questions.question: Read the passage and answer the question. 'Eight hours of daily exposure, year in and year out, to boiler-factory din would eventually result in permanent hearing loss. Then the same hazard applied to ground crews at airports and aircraft carriers.' What does the passage imply about repeated loud noise?

options.text: One loud sound always causes deafness at once
Amplifiers have no effect on hearing
Repeated exposure can cause permanent hearing loss

questions.explanation: The passage says continuous, long-term exposure to loud noise eventually causes permanent loss.

questions.question: Read the passage and answer the question. 'Otologists now report that youngsters are going deaf as a result of blasting their eardrums with electronically amplified music.' As used in the passage, 'blasting their eardrums' most nearly means:

options.text: Exposing their ears to very loud sound

questions.explanation: To blast one's eardrums is to subject them to sound so loud that it damages hearing.

questions.question: Read the passage and answer the question. 'The approach to the University is being restructured to ease the flow of traffic, give better security and provide an appropriate introduction to a seat of higher learning. The Works and Services Complex is also under construction, and we intend to move into the completed (major) part of it within the next few weeks. All these projects are being executed with an eye to aesthetics for we recognize the important influence of a beautiful and healthy environment of its inhabitants and feel that a cluster of buildings on a small space such as we have should be so well designed as to have a beneficial psychological and sociological effect on all members of the community. I have gone to these lengths to itemize these examples of current development for two main reasons. Firstly, to advise you that the road diversions and other physical inconveniences currently being experienced will be on the increase because of intense development activity. We therefore appeal to you to bear with us in full knowledge and consolation that such inconveniences are temporary and will soon yield final tangible results. Secondly, to demonstrate our capacity for executing approved projects with dispatch, and to assure Government that we are up to the task. Indeed, I can assure Government that its ability to disburse funds to us will be more than matched by our capacity to collect and expend them on executing various worthy projects in record time.' From the passage, we can gather that the inconveniences suffered by the people will be:

options.text: A sign that health is not considered
A deliberate attempt to inconvenience people
A result of buildings being put up anyhow

questions.explanation: The writer says the inconveniences are temporary and will yield real results.

questions.question: Read the passage and answer the question. 'I can assure Government that its ability to disburse funds to us will be more than matched by our capacity to collect and expend them on executing various worthy projects in record time.' Unless it can be shown that money voted for projects can be spent on them in good time, what would follow?

options.text: The development activity would not be intense
It would not be easy to convince the Government of the university's executive ability
It would not be difficult to ask the Government for funds
The final results would be unreliable

questions.explanation: The assurance rests on the university's demonstrated capacity to collect and spend project funds quickly.

questions.question: Read the passage and answer the question. 'All these projects are being executed with an eye to aesthetics.' As used in the passage, 'an eye for aesthetics' means:
questions.explanation: Aesthetics concerns beauty, so an eye for aesthetics means designing with beauty in mind.

questions.question: Read the passage and answer the question. 'I have itemised these examples of current development for two main reasons: to warn of increased inconvenience and to show our capacity for executing approved projects.' Which statement is NOT one of the reasons given by the author for enumerating the current developments?

options.text: To show the university is capable of executing approved projects
To convince the Government that the university can be trusted with the task
To say the inconvenience will go on indefinitely
To show the university can complete worthy projects within the scheduled time

questions.explanation: The writer says the inconvenience is temporary; indefinite inconvenience is the opposite of the stated reason.

questions.question: Read the passage and answer the question. 'This awareness is shown in such behavioural acts as disobedience and the use of the word No with emphasis, because the child is aware that he does not have to obey parental commands.' What main difference is mentioned between the child and the adult?
questions.explanation: The adult can weigh consequences because she has a concept of time; the child does not.

questions.question: Read the passage and answer the question. 'The two-year-old child begins to refuse orders because he is aware he does not have to obey parental commands.' Why does the two-year-old begin to refuse orders?

options.text: Because he does not understand them
Because he has merely learnt the word 'No'

questions.explanation: Refusal follows the child's awareness that he is a separate self and need not obey every command.

questions.question: Read the passage and answer the question. 'The psychologist means that the child is aware that he is a self and not an extension of his mother.' What kind of awareness does the child demonstrate at two?

options.text: That he does not love his mother
Consciousness of all things around him
That he should think of himself alone
That he is different and separate from others

questions.explanation: It is awareness of being a self apart from the mother, not mere responsiveness or knowledge of the world.

questions.question: Read the passage and answer the question. 'The chance that a black male between the ages of 15 and 19 will be killed by a gun has almost tripled since 1985, and almost doubled for white males. The writer says the firearms figures are rising because more teenagers are now getting killed by firearms than used to.' From the passage, what can be inferred since 1985?

options.text: More black males aged 15 to 19 have been getting killed by guns
More white than black males have been getting killed by guns
More black males aged 15 to 19 have been killing one another with guns
More black than white males have been killing one another with guns

questions.explanation: The passage says the chance of being killed by a gun has almost tripled for that age group; it does not say the victims are each other.

questions.question: Read the passage and answer the question. 'Secretary Donna Shalala pronounced the statistics frightening and intolerable.' In Secretary Shalala's view, the situation depicted by the statistics is:
questions.explanation: Frightening means alarming, and intolerable means unbearable.

questions.question: Read the passage and answer the question. 'The firearms figures are rising because more teenagers are now getting killed by firearms than used to.' Why does the writer say the firearms figures are rising?

options.text: More teenagers are now killed by firearms than by motor accidents
More teenagers are getting killed by firearms than used to
Firearms now have extremely high figures

questions.explanation: The writer defines rising figures as more teenage firearm deaths than in the past.

questions.question: Read the passage and answer the question. 'If the premise of education is granted — that good models can influence the young — then bad models can have an equivalent harmful effect.' What would actually be proved if the premise of education is granted?

options.text: Violence on television encourages violence in real life
Good models can influence the young
Entertainment on television is harmful to society
The viewer of fantasised violence is the criminal who acts it out

questions.explanation: If good models influence the young, the self-evident bad counterpart is that violent television models encourage real-life violence.

questions.question: Read the passage and answer the question. 'Witness enough mimed shootouts and see enough corpses fall across the screen, and the taking of a human life seems no big deal. Is not this numbed sensitivity and overkill reason enough for cutting back on films and television?' In the passage, 'numbed sensitivity' refers to:

options.text: Heartlessness on the part of actors
Deadening of the capacity to feel

questions.explanation: Suppose constant screen violence numbs sensitivity: human life as seen on screen then feels like 'no big deal'.

questions.question: Read the cloze passage and choose the word that best completes the gap. 'Drought is a word that invokes strong emotions. This is not surprising as the ___ is usually accompanied by a number of unpleasant developments.'
questions.explanation: Drought is a natural phenomenon that usually brings unpleasant developments, not an abstract ideology.

questions.question: Read the cloze passage and choose the word that best completes the gap. 'These developments have ___ for all citizens, starting from peasant farmers to state and federal governments.'
questions.explanation: 'Results' is the ordinary word for what developments produce for people.

questions.question: Read the cloze passage and choose the word that best completes the gap. 'Governments which may be plunged into emergency and crisis, which, if not successfully ___, could result in social unrest.'
questions.explanation: A crisis must successfully be managed.

questions.question: Read the cloze passage and choose the word that best completes the gap. 'The timeliness of the onset of the rains and their distribution thereafter have become ___ of considerable anxiety to all people.'
questions.explanation: Rain timing and distribution have become issues that cause anxiety.

questions.question: Read the cloze passage and choose the word that best completes the gap. 'The fact, however, is that periodic in the normal ___ of rainfall in the country is not new.'
questions.explanation: The normal supply of rainfall is a fixed collocation.

questions.question: Read the cloze passage and choose the word that best completes the gap. 'Since large areas of the country are drought-prone, the consequences are ___.'
questions.explanation: Drought consequences are disastrous, not effective or merely inevitable.

questions.question: Read the cloze passage and choose the word that best completes the gap. 'There are two aspects of coping with drought. One has to do with emergency measures and the other with ___ measures.'
questions.explanation: The contrast is between emergency measures and ordinary routine measures.

questions.question: Read the cloze passage and choose the word that best completes the gap. 'There are bound to be other lasting and ___ consequences, such as distress and sales of cattle by livestock owners in order to buy food.'
questions.explanation: 'Parallel' means running alongside and is the natural companion to lasting.

questions.question: Read the cloze passage and choose the word that best completes the gap. 'Government should provide farmers with agricultural inputs and ensure that they have easy access to these inputs under the relief ___.'
questions.explanation: 'Relief scheme' is the standard noun for an organized aid arrangement.
